messages.subject: ANOVA
parts:
Hi,

I need to do the analysis of variance on different bee sound samples (short sample is attached).

Even before I start there are some things I do not understand, perhaps somebody can help or advise me...

1.
In R Guide test sample date structure to be used for ANOVA function is like this:

 Observation Gender Dosage Alertness
1            1      m      a         8
2            2      m      a        12
3            3      m      a        13
4            4      m      a        12
5            5      m      b         6
6            6      m      b         7
7            7      m      b        23
8            8      m      b        14
9            9      f        a        15

It can be seen from spectrogram that sample data include information about amplitude, frequency and time scale (see picture1 in attached document appendix1).
However using command >head or >str it can be seen that my "test5s.wav" sample looks nothing like it:

> str(prisko)
Class 'audioSample'  atomic [1:114992] -0.0677 -0.0628 -0.0699 -0.0627 -0.0682 ...
  ..- attr(*, "rate")= int 22050
  ..- attr(*, "bits")= int 16

> head(prisko)
sample rate: 22050Hz, mono, 16-bits
[1] -0.06769005 -0.06283761 -0.06994842 -0.06274606 -0.06823939 -0.06860561

Correct me if I am wrong but should my data not look something like below structure in order to be able to use it for analysis of variance?

            Time Frequency Amplitude
1            1          x               y
2            2          x               y
3            3          x               y
4            4          x               y
5            5          x               y
6            6          x               y
7            7          x               y
8            8          x               y
9            9          x               y

So how do I transform my "chaos" data in any kind of "organized" data that can be used for analysis?

2.
Since analysis of variance is not my strong side I was wondering if anyone could give me some advice on how to approach it?
We want to avoid noise and ehcoes so we need to restrict our analysis to fequencies between 0.2 and 0.4 (rough estimation).
Can I use same rectangular sections of different sound samples and compare it (see picture2,example A) or do I need to take multiple crossesection data from one sample and compare it to same crossections of another sample see (picture2,example B). My mentor wants to do it like example B but I am not sure why this would be better approach and what is so good about it...?

This is all for now, hope to receive some useful advice, thx for your help,

Dragan

messages.author: dba8d1ebc846c330
messages.subject: Re: [Rkoholiki] ANOVA
parts:
Dear Dragan,

1. You did not define the factor with which you want to compare with in the sample set.

          SampleID Time Frequency Amplitude
1            a                1          x               y
2            a                2          x               y
3            a                3          x               y
4            a                4          x               y
5            a                5          x               y
6            b                1          x               y
7            b                2          x               y
8            b                3          x               y
9            b                4          x               y

2. I do not get completely your aim of the comparison. Do you want to compare dominant frequency (the frequency with the highest amplitude), average ampitude, or something else? In sound analysis the former is mostly used. Than we can ask the question whether you want to compare for instance dominant frequencies and its amplitude between samples (A) or amplitude on different selected frequencies between samples (B). In method B you have a selected number of frequencies which you want to measure the amplitude. This can be useful when you already know the frequency distribution and where the frequencies with the higher amplitudes are. When you would only do three cross sections like described in method B it is possible that you miss the highest frequency. It might be therefore be better to ask yourself the question whether there are differences in dominant frequency between the samples. For this you will need more rectangles (one rectangle would be an influx of frequency (it is not really clear what the sound sample is and what the influxes of frequency stand for)) randomly chosen within one sample. Optimal is more than 30 but 10 is also ok.  However, this also increases to chance for statistical difference, which make biological no sense. Be aware that sample closer in time are more similar than later in time. This creates dependency among eachother. Measurements sampled in time can be more independent when there is a larger time gap in between. I don't know how large this should be for bees.

When you got the data which is needed, you have to check whether the response variables (frequency and amplitude) are normally distributed per sample. This you can check with a histogram. If this is the case you can use an ANOVA if not you can (log or square root) transform the data and hope it will be normally distributed and do an ANOVA. If this is not the case, you can use the non parametric Kruskal wallis test, which can also compare differences between more samples, but is more robust than the ANOVA. After that you will know that there is a difference between the samples, but not where is the difference. For this you can use a post hoc test. For the ANOVA you can use the Tukey test (TukeyHSD(ANOVA output))and with the Kruskal Wallis test there is a post hoc test in the package "pgirmess".

If you have more questions or remarks please let me know. If you like we can discuss this eye to eye, I will this afternoon at the R course otherwise we can meet in biološko središče on another time of the day.

Kind regards,

Maarten

seems you really know your way around statistical analysis of data.

It also looks like that my initial email lacks to define what my question actually is, like Roman mentioned.

The reason may very well be that I did not really know how to ask the question but fortunately your answeres have some of the key vocabulary that I can use to describe my issue.

1.
The key for sure is to find out how amplitude changes with regards to frequency - I agree that most useful frequency to be used for this is dominant frequency, but will this be enough? I think I should use more freqencies, if this will give me more complete picture of  sound analysis than only comparing dominant frequency? Will it? As I discused this with my mentor at the time we were recording he also did not want to limit comparing of results solely on dominant frequency.

2.
But since I want to compare how bee sound amplitudes change with regards to relevant frequencies while bees are exposed to different factors (alcohol, insecticides, wheather...) I must assume that dominant frequency will not always be the same, so from this point of view rectangle data that does not relate to single frequency might be better?

Your second paragraph is really heavy - you really know how to do statistical analysis. Since you mention we can meet eye to eye I would gladly accept this since writing this stuff is really something else than discussing it eye to eye. I can make necessary arrangements at work so you can propose any other day and time, whatever is ok for you.

Kind regards,

Dragan
